newsitem.title: UK: IRA truce starts in N.Ireland, arms row continues.
newsitem.headline: IRA truce starts in N.Ireland, arms row continues.

text.p: An IRA ceasefire in its war against Britain took effect at midday on Sunday, overshadowed by threats from pro-British Unionists to boycott talks which the nationalist guerrillas' spokesmen are now on track to join.

The IRA truce, announced on Saturday, formally halted a 28-year war against British rule of Northern Ireland and will allow its Sinn Fein political wing to take part in the talks in six weeks if the ceasefire is deemed genuine by Britain.

But Unionists, who want Northern Ireland to stay British, threatened to walk out of the year-long negotiations in a row over ground rules which will allow Sinn Fein to take part without the IRA surrendering a single bullet first.

The leader of the mainstream Ulster Unionist Party (UUP), David Trimble, kept silent ahead of a meeting with British Prime Minister Tony Blair on Monday which could determine whether his party, the province's biggest, stays at the negotiations. "We will be going (to see Blair) with an open mind. We will be fearful of the outcome nonetheless," the UUP's security spokesman Ken Maginnis told reporters.

But he could not conceal his anger at Anglo-Irish proposals that will relegate the surrender of arms held by the IRA and its Protestant Loyalist foes to a sub-committee of the negotiations alongside a search for a political settlement.
"I don't have the right to pollute democracy in this way," said Maginnis, describing Sinn Fein president Gerry Adams as "the leader of Europe's biggest terrorist organisation."
Adams says that the legal party which he leads is separate from the IRA.
Peter Robinson, deputy leader of the smaller Democratic Unionist Party, said he would aim to block the "arms decommissioning" proposals when the talks resume on Wednesday.
"We would not take part in a process with those who are wedded to violence," he told the BBC.

The two Unionist parties believe that the IRA truce is a tactical ploy and both spokesmen pointed to a report in the Dublin Sunday Tribune which said that IRA commanders had been told it would last only four months and then be reviewed.

They cited as proof an IRA statement heralding the August 1994 ceasefire which also promised a "total cessation" but was followed 17 months later by an IRA bombing campaign when Sinn Fein was barred from the talks in a row over decommissioning.
"Unless we get disarmament, unless we get people committed to consent, we cannot expect that this is going to be other than the farce it was two years ago," Maginnis said.
A 17-year-old Catholic was shot in both legs in an IRA-style "punishment shooting" on Saturday, 24 hours before the guerrillas' truce tooks effect, police said.

The shooting was typical of the kind of violence IRA squads patrolling their own areas hand out to wayward youths every year and which are supposed to stop under British demands for an end to all violence in the province.

There was little public euphoria. Church services were held across the province and in the neighbouring Irish Republic but jubilation was tempered by the realisation that the political negotiations may become the next battlefield.

Martin McGuinness, Sinn Fein's chief negotiator, said Unionists, who speak for the 60 percent Protestant majority, had to learn to accept change after 75 years of being the dominant force in the province's turbulent politics.
"I think the problem with the Unionists is that they dont want to come to the negotiating table because they don't want change," he told Sky news.
He urged them to follow the example of South Africa and the Middle East where peace talks were started without any arms surrender by the protagonists.
"What we have got to do is put the horse before the cart," said McGuinness, who is said by aides to have the best contacts with the underground IRA.

"In all countries throughout the world, many people have dealt with this issue, many like (former south African President F.W.) de Klerk in South Africa and others in the conflict in the middle east have accepted these issues need to be pragmatically dealt with."
John Hume, leader of the Social Democratic and Labour Party, a moderate Irish nationalist group, urged all Unionists to accept that violence had ended with the IRA truce.
"They (the IRA) could have over 1,000 guns on Monday and buy 1,000 more on Tuesday. The real question is to get the violence stopped," he said.
